Rationalisation of Excise Duty for Textile Industry 
4293. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any representation from the Indian 
Cotton Mills Federation, New Delhi regarding rationalisation of excise duty 
for textile industry; 
(b) if so, the details of issues raised in their representation thereof; 
(c) whether Government have taken up this representation for active 
consideration; 
(d) if so, what is the Government's reaction thereto; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor and by when action is likely to be taken in 
the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) The Indian Cotton Mills 
Federation (ICMF) had sent pre-budget representations regarding rationalisation 
of excise duty for textile fabrics. The issues raised by them included completion 
of the CENVAT chain covering all stages of manufacture from fibres to garments, 
allowing of the CENVAT credit at the processed fabric stage of actuals basis and 
discontinuing the system of deemed CENVAT credit,  withdrawal of excise 
exemptions of hank yam, hand processed textile fabrics when power is used for 
specified finishing processes, knitwear s and readymade garm ents in the SSI 
sector, abolition of optional stentor duty for independent textile processors 
and rationalization of excise duty structure on fibres and yarns, fabrics, made-
up and ready-made garments. 
100 

[7 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) The Government have considered all the representations 
received from the textile industry including that from ICMF in the budget and 
have announced a special package of incentives for the textile industry. These 
include reduction of excise duty on fabrics, made-ups and garments from 16% to 
12%, withdrawal of excise exemption on hank yam, restricting the exemption 
on hand processed fabrics on use of power to 7/4 specified processes, levy of 
excise duty on optional basis on grey fabrics, cotton knitted fabrics and knitwears, 
abolition of optional compounded levy scheme for independent textile 
processors and exemption from excise duty on automatic looms and specified 
textile processing machinery. 
(e) Does not arise in view of reply to parts (c) and (d) above.

Lock-in period on sale proceeds by NRIs 
4297. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Reserve Bank has removed the lock-in-period of three 
years for repatriation of sale proceeds by NRIs/PIOs; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefore; and 
(c) what would be the inflow and outflow of foreign exchange so envisaged in this 
behalf for the next three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) In terms of Regulation 6 of RBI's 
Notification No. 21/2000/RB dated May 3, 2000, NRIs and PIOs, have been permitted 
to repatriate sale proceeds of immovable property subject to certain conditions, inter-
alia, that the property is sold after 3 years from the date of acquisition or from the date 
of payment of final instalment whichever is later. As a result NRIs/PIOs who have-
entered into contracts to purchase properties in India are unable to take back their 
money unless they have paid full amount of purchase in the circumstances even in the 
cases where construction work is not progressing satisfactorily or for some compelling 
reasons the buyer has to cancel the contract, the funds brought in by the NRIs are 
blocked in India. In order to mitigate the difficulties faced by NRIs/PIOs Reserve Bank 
has decided henceforth to allow repatriation of sale proceeds or amount received on 
account of cancellation of purchase contracts, subject to the condition that the amount 
does not exceed amount paid for acquisition of the property in foreign exchange brought 
through Banking Channel or the amount realized whichever is lesser.

transferred and posted to non-sensitive charges and are also not selected for

(a) whether it is a fact that the ratio of net Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) 
of Public Sector Banks is 2.26 per cent of total assets but in case of foreign binks 
it is only 0.79 per cent; 
(b) if so, whether this vast difference is attributable to management of the 
PSBs vis-a-vis foreign banks or whether there are any other reasons for this; and 
(c) whether any study has been made for recovery of NPAs during the last 
three years and whether any changes are required to improve the recovery of 
NPAs? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) The ratio of net NPAs to total assets of 
Public Sector Banks (PSBs) as on March 31,2001 was 2.72% and 0.8% for Foreign 
Banks. The major reasons for difference in ratio of net NPAs to total assets of 
PSBs and foreign banks is that the foreign banks operating in selected locations 
lend to selected clientele in selected areas with priority sector lending limited to 
export credit and credit to  SSI Sector. The PSBs with large rural network are 
required to lend to all sections of the society including agriculture, education, 
housing, Government sponsored schemes, weaker sections and other priority 
sectors as well. 
(c) Government and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reviews the position of 
NPAs on a continuing basis and various measures have been taken for recovery 
of NPAs such as evolving and implementation of recovery policy by banks for 
110 

 
[7 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
restructuring, reschedutement and compromise settlement, filing of suits in DRTs 
and Courts, vigorous monitoring, supervision and follow up of Non-Performing 
Assets (NPAs) at various levels by the management. Further, Corporate Debt 
Restructuring mechanism has been put in place. Action has also been taken for 
setting up of Asset Reconstruction Companies. Legislative changes are proposed 
to facilitate securitisation, foreclosures and enforcement of securities in cases 
of default with the intervention of the Court. 
NABARD guidelines for rural banks 
4306. SHRI C. P.THTRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state. 
(a) whether NABARD has issued guidelines to improve functioning of 
Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks in the States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the NABARD has examined the problem faced by Cooperative 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks in various States; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) National Bank for Agriculture and 
Rural Development (NABARD) has reported that it has issued guidelines and 
taken a number of initiatives for improving the working of the State Cooperative 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs). These measures include 
preparation of institution-specific development action plans (DAPs) aimed at 
attaining current/sustainable viability in the shortest possible time-frame and 
implementation and monitoring the same through the mechanism of Memorandum 
of Understanding (MoU). These guidelines were revised in July, 2000 for 
incorporating implementation of prudential norms (income recognition, asset 
classification and provisioning norms), etc. Guidelines were further issued in 
April,2001 for implementing one-time stetement scheme (OTS) to reduce the 
level of non- performing assets. 
(c) to (e) Government had set up a task Force to stud y the cooperative 
credit system and suggest measures for its strengthening under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Jagdish Capoor. The Task Force found that SCARDBs were suffering 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2002] 
from duality of control, lack of professional management, high intermediation 
cost, low profitability/losses, poor recovery, high levels of non-performing 
assets, etc. The Task Force recommende d a four dimensional revitalization 
package encompassing financial, operational, organization and systematic 
aspects including recapitalisation of po tentially viable cooperative credit 
institutions. Subsequently, a committee under the Chairmanship of Minister of 
State for Finance had been constituted for consideration of revitalization 
assistance to cooperative banks. Subsequent to the submission of the report by 
the Committee, Government has made a provision of Rs. 100 crore in the 
Budget for the year 2002-2003 for revitalising the cooperative banks including 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks.

4321. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a considerable fall in the interest rates/ 
Prime Lending Rates (PLR) of all commercial banks in the last few years; 
(b) if so, whether there has been any relative reduction in refinance rates 
of sponsored banks and particularly of NABARD to RRBs and cooperatives; 
(c) the details of refinance amounts and rates charged by NABARD and 
sponsored banks; and

above cost of demand deposits to serve the real purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) have reported 
that since October 1994, interest rates on advances of Rs. 2 lakhs and above 
were deregulated. The commercial banks are free to determine their own lending 
rates on advances with credit limits of over Rs. 2 lakhs. There has been a 
considerable fall in the interest rates/Prime Lending Rate (PLR) of commercial

provides short-term refinance support to State Cooperative Banks (SCBs)/ 
District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) 
for financing seasonal agricultural operations (SAO) and other than SAO out of 
the general line of credit provided to NABARD by RBI. The present refinance 
rate of NABARD for RRBs is 7.0% for SAOs. Similarly, for State Cooperative 
Banks the rates are 5.5 to 7.5%.

refinance under investment credit during 1999-2000,2000-01 and 2001-02 by

Working capital for small scale sector 
4327. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Confederation of Indian Industries has inter alia suggested 
Government to have a sub target within priority sector lending to promote 
alternative sources of finance, to establish an independent credit rating agency 
and to make the Nayak Committee norms regarding working capital applicable 
131 

RAJYA  SABHA               [7 May, 2002] 
as a rule to alleviate the capital related problems of small scale industry; 
(b) if so, whether Government have examined these suggestion; and 
(c) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) yes, sir. 
(b) and (c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that no sub-target has 
been prescribed for financing SSI Units within the priority sector lending targets. 
According to RBI, the public sector banks advances to SSI Units have shown 
steady increase in absolute terms and that even without any target, out of 40% of 
target for priority sectors, agriculture and SSI together account for 34 percentage points, 
thus leaving only 6% for the rest of other important segments of priority sectors such 
small business, retail trade, housing, education and self-employed person etc. Fixing 
sub target may result in crowding out in other priority sectors, RBI has, therefore, 
decided not to fix any sub-target for SSI within the priority sector lending. Banks 
are however being advised by RBI to fix a target for the year on year growth in 
SSI. 
As regards computation of working capital limits for SSI, Banks are 
reportedly computing the same on the basis of minimum 20% of the annual 
projected turn over upto a borrowal limit of Rs. 5 crore as per Nayak Committee 
recommendations. RBI's Study of specialized SSI and General Branches revealed that 
working capital was computed on the basis of the norms in 93% of the proposals 
received in specialized SSI Branches and about 79 percent of proposals received in 
general branches.

As a non-structural measure of flood management, a scheme namely, 
"Flood forecasting & Warning System on rivers common to India and Nepal" is 
in operation since 1989 for exchange of hydrological and meteorological data 
from Nepal to India for flood forecasts. 
Further the discussions have been conducted with Nepal on minimizing 
the effects of floods from rivers originating from Nepal in this regard a joint 
Inception Report has been finalised for Sapra Koshi High Dam Multipurpose 
Project and Sun Kosi Storage cum-diversion Scheme paving the way for setting 
up of Joint Project Officer and preparation of Joint Detailed Project Report 
having inter-alia flood control benefits for Bihar. 
In additon, in order to prevent spilling of flood waters from Lalbakeya, 
Bagmati, Khando and Kamla rivers from Nepal side into Bihar, both sides have 
agreed to extend the embankments in no man's land and work on Lalbakeya is 
nearing completion. 
For dealing with the pr oblems of inundation in the vicinity of India-
Nepal border, a Standing Committee on Inundation Problems between India 
and Nepal is also functioning since 1986. So far, twelve meetings have been 
held in which various issues have been sorted out. Apart from this, the 
Government of India has set up High Level Committees on Kosi and Gandak 
rivers to inspect and recommend measures to protect the banks of the two rivers 
in and around Kosi and Gandak barrages from erosion. 
In order to have inter-action at higher level, a Joint Committee on Water 
Resources headed by the respective Wate r Resources Secretaries of both the 
countries has also been established to oversee the entire gamut of India-Nepal 
co-operation in the Water Resources Sector. 
Recently, during March,2002, Prime Ministers of India and Nepal met in 
Delhi and amongst many other issues, matters concerning cooperation in the 
field of water resources were discussed which included matters to mitigate the 
adverse affects of floods from rivers flowing from Nepal.

(SHRIMATI BIJOYACHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b)The Government of India

sea erosion works during the period 1970-71 to 1991-92. Also, an amount of

decision taken in the 43rd meeting of National Development Council held in 
December, 1991. Further, the Government of India released Rs.3.00 crore as 
special Central Assistance as one time measure for completing anti sea erosion 
works in Kerala by June, 1996. An additional Central assistance amounting to 
Rs. 1.00 crore was provided to Government of Tamil Nadu during the financial 
year 2000-2001 and Rs.3.50 crore to Government of West Bengal during 
2001 -02 for anti sea erosion works.

SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH (Rajasthan): Mr. Chairman, Sir, when I 
joined the Indian Foreign Service 49 years ago, diplomats were told that a 
good diplomat thinks twice before saying nothing. In the past 50 years, the

content of diplomacy, the nature of diplomacy has altered the world over. In 
our country, for the past 50 years, t here has been a broad national consensus 
on the foreign policy. The framework that  Nehru constructed has survived the 
test of the time even when some super ficial and supercilious predators have 
tried to tamper with that framework. You abandon Nehru and you are left 
naked in the foreign affairs field. 
I will begin by mentioning the important link between the domestic 
policy and the foreign policy. This is mo st dramatically made available to the 
country and to the House by the recent  events in Gujarat. I will quote from a 
book written by P.N. Haksar whom the Mi nister of External Affairs, like me, 
admires very much. Nehruji said, "Foreign policies depend ultimately on 
internal conditions and developments. In ternal progress for us, therefore, 
becomes essential if we have to play an effective part in world affairs". Shri 
P.N. Haksar says, "Thus sovereignty and independence are indispensable to 
conduct of foreign policy of any nation and even if a country is sovereign and 
independent, it cannot effectively pursue a foreign policy unless it is cohesive 
within itself and consistent in its purpose." 
I have been a representativ e of India for 31 years and it has been a 
great honour to me because India has on e of the best Foreign Services in the 
world. We come to the Foreign Servic es through one of the most difficult 
competitive examinations that the world has to offer. But the instrument that 
the diplomats have to have is a clear-c ut policy framework and a leadership 
which is familiar with the foundations of India's foreign policy laid down before 
Independence; what are its sources of in spirations and what are the springs 
from which it flows. If you are not familia r with those, then you fall into the kind 
of traps we have been falling for the la st few years. One of the fundamental 
problems that the present dispensation is confronted with is they are not clear 
about what India's foreign policy is. I say this with very great respect because I 
have respect for the shrines of the minds of all the Members in this House. For 
example, take the statement made by the Prime Minister in Ahmedabad before 
going to Singapore. Sir, 120 foreign missions in Delhi reported to their 
Governments that the Prime Minister of  India has spoken like a statesman. He 
comes back and speaks in Goa. The same 120 missions send reports to their 
Governments that the Prime Minister of India has spoken like a Swayam 
Sewak. Now the Prime Minister has been facing a great dilemma ever since he 
became Prime Minister.    When is he a statesman and when is he a

that country that you have no business to interfere in our internal affairs. The 
fact of the matter is that  a large number of people of Indian region are citttens 
of the USA, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Netherlands.

the dispensation in the External Affairs Ministry is aware of the shortcomings

Let me now come to the fundamental s of India's foreign policy, that 
is, non-alignment. It has become fashionable to say that non-alignment is not 
relevant. And I have seldom heard Jaswant Singhji resorting to any reference 
to non-alignment. He has done so rarely, and I would like him to read the 
Prime Minister's speech in Durban, wh ere the Prime Minister praised non-
alignment. "The Cold War has ended, the Warsaw Pact is wound up, but 
NATO is expanding to the borders of Russia." Against whom? If non-
alignment is irrelevant, then, I think, NATO is even more irrelevant? But I will 
tell you how and why non-alignment is rele vant even today as it was 20 years 
or 40 years, ago. The international age nda has changed, which, of course, is 
inevitable. When I represented India in  the 50's and the 60's, the agenda was 
colonialism, imperialism, rationalism, a partheid and so on. Today, the agenda 
is environment, drugs, AIDS, population and ecology. So, in this arena-ll, it 
would help us if the non-aligned movement had a proper leadership, and India 
is a country which can give that leadership, which this Government is not 
giving. But, on these issues which affect the human kind, we should take a 
lead in the non-aligned movement and speak with one voice. Let me quote 
from a very distinguished European St atesman, Dr. Richard von Weizsacker, 
who was the President of Germany for 10 years. In the lecture which he 
delivered at the Nehru Memorial in 2000, he said, "Nehru was among the first 
and foremost to look for a non-bloc internationalism. His idea of non-alignment 
became of global importance. He spoke about peace clubs against Cold War-
clubs, nuclear clubs. He was pondering how to create a sort of no-war-zone 
between the military blocs. From the outset his thoughts became and 
remained fruitful. Non-alignment was aiming at more than equidistance from 
blocs.   It was a denial of the gist of bloc thinking, an endeavour to

Nations. That is what we are working for.

to assure him that there is no change in the Government's stand with regard to 
the LTTE. It is a proscribed organisation,  and the Government is fully mindful 
of not simply the sensibilities involved in this case, but the fact that we have to 
work in such a fashion that the territorial and Constitutional integrity of Sri 
Lanka is kept inviolate and, simultaneously, the aspirations of the people of Sri 
Lanka must be fulfilled.   We cannot accept any division of

Sri Lanka. And we cannot accept any exportation of the problems of Sri Lanka 
on to the Peninsula or to any part of I ndia. So far as the extradition of Mr. 
Prabhakaran is concerned, India has made a formal request for his extradition 
and we have reminded Government of Sri Lanka. This request is still pending. 
That is where the matter is, and there is change in this regard, so far as India

On the question of Pakistan, I could very easily spend half-an-hour 
discussing this issue - whether it is Lahore,  whether it is Kargil. I shall now not 
refer to it by name. But when hon. Me mbers point out that I am the guilty 
person who went to Kandahar, let me just correct  one aspect of It. I did not 
escort anyone. I have explained this clearly a number of times. Please take 
your mind back. This was the Christmas and the New Year of 1999. There 
were already two aeroplanes of Indian Airlines at the Kandahar Airfield. The 
Kandahar Airfield was not, in any case, an international airfield. It was under 
the control of Taliban. There were 166 persons on board, who had been there 
for the last seven days, on that ill-fated 814. We had definite information that if 
steps were not taken, that aircraft will be taken off in the air on 31 st December, 
and blown in the air. It was necessary for me to go because we anticipated 
that there will be last minute hitches in the rescue of those 166 passengers. 
There was no way Kandahar could take the fourth aeroplane. I chose to go. I 
volunteered to go. I volunteered to go be cause I considered it my duty to try 
and rescue those 166 persons. It was a bitter, bitter poison to swallow. But, in 
that aeroplane, I had to take others with me. Yes, if you charge me with that, I 
am guilty. You do reflect on the fact that before that, on the streets of Delhi, in 
front of the Prime Minster's house, in Press conferences, we were witnessing, 
on a daily basis, citizens rolling on street s. I do not agree with that. And, in 
retrospect, could I have done anything differently? I was able to get the 166 
people back. Some day I will be able to say that the complications that arose 
on the tarmac when I had landed made me do like that. In retrospect, if I had 
not gone, I am not sure that those 166 persons could have come back to Delhi 
before 1999 became 2000. However, Sir, that is now behind us. 
On Pakistan, let us be very clear. My gallant friend spoke of coercive 
diplomacy. It is not a subject that I can discuss in Parliament. On Pakistan, the 
issue is very clear. It is not India that has to decide what has to be done, it is 
Pakistan that has to decide what kind of long-term

relationship it wants with India. This is  the fundamental question. And, in this 
fundamental question, what we require from Pakistan is, what I had said on 
11th June, 1999, in the midst of the Kargil operation, My then counterpart, Shri 
Sartaj Azeez, had flown into Delhi, and I had said, "Reaffirm the inviolability of 
the Line of Control, withdraw your  aggression, and abandon cross-border 
terrorism." We had said, "You must abandon cross-border terrorism." What we

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Use of Water Resources for Generating Hydro-Electric Power in North 
Eastern States 
*601. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken to utilize the vast water resources for generating 
hydro-electric power in North Eastern States; 
(b) whether any decision has been taken on Siang (Dihang) project in 
the catchment area of the Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh; 
(c) whether the Brahmaputra Board has been consulted in this regard; 
and 
(d) the present status of Tipaimukh project in Manipur? 
THE MINISTER OF -STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI METHA): (a) to (d) A Staternent is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
Regarding use of Water Resources for Generating Hydro-Electric Power in 
North Eastern States 
(a) to (d) The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has assessed that 
the vast water resources of the rivers in the Northern Eastern States have a 
hydro electric power potential of 58971 MW in terms 
 
1

RAJYA  SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
of installed generating capacity. 1062 MW generating capacity has already 
been installed so far; 387 MW is under execution and 22,795 MW 
hydroelectric projects are under Stage-I and Stage-ll activities in the Central 
Sector. The CEA has recently completed a ranking study of 399 schemes 
covering all the river basins in the country. The Brahmaputra and other river 
basins in the North East account for 145 schemes which have been ranked in 
three categories in terms of their attractiveness. Out of these, 41 schemes 
(5718 MW) have been ranked in the first category and 86 schemes (41203 
MW) in the second category. The rank ing study would enable potential 
developers to undertake detailed survey & investigation and execution of the 
viable schemes in a phased manner. CEA is holding discussions with the 
States to draw up an action plan fo r development of the identified hydro 
electric projects in the Region. The G overnment of India is according high 
priority to development of the hydro electric potential in the country, 
especially in the North Eastern Re gion. The Central Sector Public 
Undertakings, namely, the North Eastern Electric power Corporation 
(NEEPCO) and the National Hydro-elect ric Power Corporation (NHPC) are 
actively engaged in this task. NEEPCO has recently commissioned the 
Doyang Hydro Electric project (75 MW) in Nagaland and Ranganadi Hydro-
electric Project (405 MW) in Arunachal pradesh. It  is presently executing 
Kopili Stage-ll (25 MW) in Assam and Turial Hydro-electric Project (60 
MW) in Mizoram. It has also comm enced pre-construction activity on 
Kameng Hydroelectric Project (600 M W) in Arunachal Pradesh. NHPC has 
taken up, after formal transfer from the Ministry of Water Resources and due 
consultations with Brahmaputra Board, survey & investigation of Subansiri 
Upper, Middle and Lower Hydro-elect ric Schemes (total 6500 MW) and 
Siang (Dihang) Upper, Middle and Lower Hydro-electric Schemes (total 
13400 MW). The Stage-ll activities rela ting to pre-construction activities in 
respect of Subansiri Lower HE Proj ect (2000 MW) in Arunachal Pradesh 
have been approved. 
The Tipimukh Hydro-electric Proj ect (1500 MW) in Manipur was 
initially investigated by the Brahmaputra Board. The Project was handed 
over to NEEPCO in July, 1999. NEEPCO submitted the Detailed Project 
Report to the Central Electricity Authority and the Government of Manipur 
in December, 2000. It has been advi sed to tie-up necessary inputs and 
clearances for taking up implementation 
2 

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
of the project. All possible efforts are being made by NEEPCO with the help 
of the Government of Manipur to generate public opinion in favour of the 
project so as to facilitate necessary statutory clearances for the project. As the 
project entails a substantial expenditure  on account of secu rity arrangements, 
the matter is being pursued for excluding the cost of security from the project 
cost.

Power will implement in all-pervasive plan to tap fully the vast potential of 
generating hydro-electric power from uninterrupted supply of natural water 
resources of the North-East region? What is the time-frame? This is my first 
supplementary.

*602. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHME D KHAN (DURRU) : Will the 
Minister of POWER be pleased to state : 
(a) what progress has so for been made in the implementation of the 
Parbati-Hydro-electric Project (2051 MW); 
10 

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA    SABHA 
(b) the share of power allocation fo rm the project to Rajasthan, 
Himachal Pradesh and other States and on what terms; 
(c) whether there still persists any dispute about the allocations of 
power among the States; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken by Government to 
resolve the dispute as per the Memorandum of Understanding signed in the 
beginning of 1992? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) to  (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
Regarding implementation of Parbati Hydro-electric Project : The 
National Hydro-electric Power Corpor ation (NHPC) has executed an 
Agreement with Government of Himachal Pradesh on 20.11.1998 for 
development of 2051 MW of hydro-electric power project in three stages on 
river Parbati in Kullu District of Himachal Pradesh. 
The Government of India accorded approval in Decem ber, 1999 for 
taking up survey and investigation activities and preparation of Detialed 
Project Report (DPR) of the Parbati HE Project State-ll (800 MW) by NHPC 
for a cost of Rs. 77.62 crores. NHPC completed the survey and investigation 
activities and prepared a revised DPR for Parbati HE Project Stage-ll (800 
MW) which was submitted to Central Electricity Authority (CEA) in 
October, 2000. CEA accorded Techno Economic Clearance (TEC) to the 
project in January, 2001. The process for obtaining investment decision to the 
cost estimate of the Parbati HE Project Stage-ll has been initiated. 
A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) had earlier been drawn on 
20.10.1992 amongst the State of Rajast han, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana and 
Gujarat and National Capital Territory of Delhi for investigation and 
execution of Parbati Hydro-electric Project Stage-ll and Stage-Ill and 
investigation of Parbati Stage-I HE  Project and also the associated 
transmission system. This MoU had provided that 12 per cent of energy 
generated from the project shall be gi ven to Himachal Pradesh free to cost 
and the remaining 88 per cent of 
11 

RAJYA  SABHA  [8 May, 2002] 
energy generated from the project was to be apportioned amongst the States, 
including Himachal Pradesh in the ratio of their equity participation. 
In July, 1998, the Chief Minister, Himachal Pradesh conveyed to the 
Partner States of MoU of 1992 that th e agreement entered in 1992 was not 
workable as some of the States had no t been contributing their due share of 
equity, and as an alternative the Go vernment of Himachal Pradesh and 
decided after considerable thought th at the execution of the project be 
entrusted to a Central Public Sector Undertaking such as NHPC. Accordingly 
the Agreement was signed between the Government of Himachal Pradesh and 
NHPC on 20.11.1998 for execution of the three stages of the project in the 
Central Sector. 
The Government of Himachal Prades h also informed the Government 
of India that after the communication of July 1998 entrusting the execution of 
the project to a CPSU, the signing of the Agreement with NHPC on 
20.11.1998, the MoU of 20.10.1992 stands abrogated. 
The sharing of power generated from the Parbati Projects amongst the 
States/Union Territories in the Northern Region would be in keeping with the 
sharing guidelines applicable for Central Sector hydro stations.

Delay in Development of Indigenous LCA and Upgradation of 
MiG-21 
*603. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of DEFENCE - 
to pleased to state: 
(a) whether there has been inordinate delay in development of 
indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) and upgradation of MiG-21 
aircraft; 
(b) whether it is a fact that due to this delay the Indian Air Force has 
suffered a lot in air crashes and killings of pilots; and 
(c) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
There has been some delay in LCA Project which is mainly due to lack of 
development experience, non-availability of ready infrastructure, foreign 
exchange (FE) crunch of 1992, sanctions imposed by USA in 1998 and 
technological complexities. The first technology demonstrator has flow on 4th 
January, 2001 and successfully demonstrated to international experts during 
Aero India 2001. Further development is in progress for its timely induction 
in Indian Air Force. The upgradtion of MiG-21 aircraft was delayed due to 
various technical problems, integration and achieving performance 
parameters on two prototypes at Russia. The series upgradation and 
delivering to Indian Air Force has commenced at Hindustan Aeronautics 
Limited. 
(b) Non-availabiiity of LCA and delay in upgradation of MiG-21 
aircraft has not resulted in any way in increase of flying accidents. 
(c) Does not arise.

*605. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHAR JEE : Will the Minister of 
HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that the North-Eastern and Eastern States were 
recently alerted about the possible infiltration of ha rd core terrorists from 
Nepal and Bangladesh; 
(b) if so, details thereof; 
27

(c) whether the concerned State Government have beefed up security 
in their respective territories as per the advice of the Central Government; 
(d) whether the Central Government have taken up the matter with 
Nepal and Bangladesh in this regard; and 
(e) if so, their reaction and if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME 
AFFAIRS (SHRI I.D. SWAMI) : (a) to (e) The State Governments of North-
East and West Bengal as well as Ce ntral Para-Military Forces-Special 
Service Bureau (SSB) personnel deployed on Indo-Nepal border and Border 
Security Force deployed on Indo-Bangladesh borders have been advised 
about effective guarding of international border areas to check the infiltration 
of terrorists from the neighbouring countries, including, Nepal and 
Bangladesh. The concerned State Governments have alerted their police 
authorities posted in all the border districts. 
Besides, a series of measures have been taken by the Government to 
curb the illegal cross border movement of militants. These include raising of 
additional battalions Security Force, reduction of gaps between the border 
outposts, intensification of patrolling both on the land and the riverine border, 
increase in the number of outpost towers, provision of surveillance 
equipments, accelerated programme of construction of border roads and 
fencing.

countries , including, Bangladesh and Nepal. They have assured that they will 
not allow undesirable elements to use their territory for activities prejudicial 
to this interests of India.

located at Sanu, Jaisalmer District of Rajasthan. The fire broke out when the

resulting in explosion of ammunition stored inside the tank. The tank along 
with integral weapons, ammunitions and other operational stores was

caused due to short circuit in the electric systems of the tank and was not due 
to any terrorist activity.

Commanders have been advised to observe extreme caution while handling 
equipments loaded with ammunition or fuel and take adequate preventive 
measures. These would include proper insultation and connection of wiring 
circuitry of the tanks, ensure that batte ries are properly secured and leads do 
not short circuit, connections of additional Radio Sets are properly secured, 
there is no contact of inflammable materi al with fuel or ammunition, there is 
proper storage of ammunition in the tanks and regular inspection of tanks by 
Commanders and formation repair teams. 
In order to avoid recurrence of fire incidents in ammunition depots, the 
following steps have been taken: 
(a) all depots have been directed to update safety and security 
instructions. 
(b) all depots have been inspected by  a Board of Officers to check 
adequacy of safety and security arrangements. 
(c) Shortage in fire-fighting equipment is being made up and defective 
equipments repaired.

(d) In order to review the potentially viable sick textile mills which may or 
may not be closed, and with a view to timely detection of sick and potentially 
sick companies and for the speedy dete rmination of preventive ameliorative 
and remedial measures which need to be taken in respect of such companies 
the Government of India has enacted th e Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provisions) Act, 1985 and established and Board for Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction (BIFR). The rehabilitation schemes sanctioned by

BIFR include various measures like rest ructuring the capital, indication of 
fresh funds by the promoters, merger with the other companies, change of 
management, provision for working capital and term loans by banks and 
financial institutions. 
As on 31.3.2002, there were 2067 cotton/man-made fibre spinning, 
composite and exclusive weaving textile mills in the Non-SSI Sector and

problems etc.

Tapping of wind energy 
4453. SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN:  Will the Minister of NON-

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE NON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) The gross wind

the country. Wind power projects are mainly set up as commercial projects 
through private investments. The setting up of wind power capacity mainly 
depends on the availability of financing on attractive terms and a suitable 
policy for these projects in potential States.

power projects. Soft loans are also available from Indian Renewable Energy 
Development Agency (IREDA) for wind power projects.

†4459. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: W ill the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state:

(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) The States have accepted the 
need for power sector reforms. A consensus was reached in the Conference of

depoliticize power sector reforms and speed up their 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

implementation. It was resolved in th e conference to achieve break even in 
distribution in two years time and achiev e positive returns thereafter. It was

be made functional and tariff petition filed and subsidy may be given only to 
the extent of State Government's capacity to pay the subsidies explicitly 
through budget. The Government of India has signed Memoranda of

of power from Central Generating Stations and financial assistance for 
strengthening of subtransmission and distribution as well as for renovation 
and modernization of thermal and hydel power plants. 12 State Electricity 
Regulatory Commission have passed tariff orders which reflect a trend 
towards tariff rationalisation. It is expected that with the reform and 
restructuring of power sector, the confidence of investors in power sector will 
improve.

Department of Land Resources in Ministry of Rural Development is 
implementing three major Watershed Development Programmes namely, 
Integrated Watershed Development Programme (IWDP), Drought Prone 
Area Programme (DPAP) and Desert Development Programme (DDP) on 
watershed basis. These programmes aim at in-situ soil amd moisture

traditional water sources and thereby making more water available for 
agricultural and human consumption.

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY):   Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend  the Code of Civil Procedure, 
1908 and to provide for matters connected therewith or 
incidental thereto, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, originally, the Code of Civ il Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997, 
was introduced in this hon. House, on the basis of which the Bill was approved 
in the year 1999. But, before the amendments could be notified, there was a 
protest by some sect :ons of the Bar all over the country. And the then Law 
Minister, my distinguished predecessor, Shri Jethmalani, made 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
a statement in this hon. House that the law would not be notified. There was 
also a request from various sections of the House that some provisions of it 
may, perhaps, require a reconstruction. 
It was stated at that time that discussions would be held with the Bar 
and, thereafter, if any amendments were  necessitated, the same would be 
introduced in the hon. House. Sir, ther eafter, I had a series of meetings with 
the representatives of the Bar, representatives of  the Bar Council of India and 
other Bar associations, with the Law Commission; and, after the series of 
meetings that we had, some amendments to the Bill which were approved by 
this hon. House in the year 1999, we re introduced by me. These amendments 
were then referred to the Standing Committee. The Standing Committee, after 
approving a large number of them, had suggested some alterations with 
regard to some of them. I will just elaborate as to which we have been able to 
accept. If i may just give the nutshel l of what the impact of the proposed 
amendments is, as introduced by me in the year 2000, which are also 
amendments either to the principal Civ il Procedure Code or amendments to 
the proposal which was approved in the year 1999; and, on the basis of the 
recommendations of the Standing Co mmittee, what changes we have 
introduced. Sir, these are broadly in the following categories. In the first 
instance, we have now introduced a pr ovision which was not there in the 
original CPC or in the 1999 amendm ent, which states that a court, while 
regulating its hearing, will be entitled to fix and allocate the time required for 
oral hearing, that is for oral arguments, and may also give an opportunity to the 
parties to supplement the rest of t heir submissions in writing. The second 
aspect is - this is intended really to cut down delays because, as we see, the 
entire problem of judicial reforms in Indi a, one of the principal criticisms which 
is made against us, is that our procedur es are awfully slow -- now there is no 
time limit on the delivery of judgments by the court, and, therefore, it has been 
suggested that judgments should be delive red within 30 days of the hearing; 
and in case an extension of time is required for reasons which the judge will 
record, it can be extended ordinarily but not beyond a period of 60 days. 
The third amendment which was not there in the original Bill, but 
which is on the basis of the 144 th Report of the Law Commission is this. There 
were conflicting judgments by various High Courts as to whether a court can 
execute a decree outside its own jurisdicti on. We have clarified that it cannot. 
The second also is intended to remove a possible confusion on account of the 
Report of the Law Commission that if any attachment order  is  passed  by  a  
court,   and  a  transfer  of  property  takes  place 
192 

[8 May> 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
subsequent to the attachment, then this tr ansfer of property itself will be void 
and will not affect the earlier attachment which has already taken place. Sir, 
one of the criticisms which was made  against the 1999 amendment was that 
there were certain categories of orders passed by a single judge of the High 
Court against which no right of appeal was given; and the right of appeal 
which was there originally had been taken away, particularly, orders passed 
under articles 226 and 227. That right we  are restoring, that is, against every 
judicial order which is passed, at leas t, one right of appeal would be there to 
correct an error into which the single judge could have fallen. But where a 
single judge exercises an appellate jurisdiction, against that, the second right 
of appeal before a Division Bench is not provided. 
Sir, there is also a considerable am ount of delay which is noticed in 
the case of service of summons. The 1999 amendment made one very 
progressive change that, it allowed various other methodologies of service, 
other than the traditional methods, thro ugh process fee and court processes, 
etc., and by registered post; it allowe d electronic transmission of service of 
summons. But now, we have found that in addition to the postal services, 
there are parallel courier services which are being run across the country, and, 
in some cases, service of summons itself takes very long time. We have, 
therefore, said that every court, whether it is a High Court or a district court, 
will have a panel of approved courier service agencies which will also be 
entitled to serve summons. Their experienc e of the system has been that they 
have been quite expeditious in the process of serving. 
Sir, there were two points of criticism which were made against the 
1999 Bill. One was that there was a fixed time of 30 days which was given for 
filing a response to a case. The Bar Associations had expressed an opinion 
that if you have a fixed time, with no pr ovision, in any exigency, for extension 
of that time, then there could be a hardship caused in certain cases, 
particularly, to the poorer sections of the society; people may have to arrange 
for money to pay their lawyer's fee; people in rural areas may actually require 
to travel to district headquarters in  order to engage lawyers, collect all 
documents, collect all fa cts; there may be cases where a person may be 
unwell and, therefore, for him to file it in 30 days, under all circumstances, may 
not be possible; and if he does not file it in 30 days, adverse consequences 
would be attracted because the judge is powerless, if he does not file his reply 
within 30 days. 
We have now said that, ordinarily, it should have to be filed within 
thirty days; but a discretion has been given to a judge to extend this period

further by sixty days, not more than sixty days, for special reasons, if he has to 
record in writing. So, the ordinary period of reply will remain* thirty days, with 
some power of extension, which a judge may himself have. 
Similarly, Sir, the power of am endment of a pleading, whidh was 
taken away by the 1999 Amendment, also attracted a lot of commerrt, 
particularly, because in some cases,  new factors may arise. The law may 
change. Subsequent facts may arise in a given case, which it may be 
necessary in the interest of justice, to  bring it to the notice of the court. And

1999, which we have now introduced. The longest duration which is taken in 
the life of a case, is in the recording of evidence itself. When evidence is

said, "That the examination in chief will be on affidavit, which was also

factors, which the judge may 
194 

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
take into consideration. There may be  a subject matter where the judge feels

where he feels that it can be delegated a nd instead of taking years before a 
court, we have also made a provision that when it is submitted before a 
commissioner, in whom the power is delegated, whose calendar is not as long 
as that of an ordinary court is, then normally, unless the period is extended, 
the commissioner will try to return the record of evidence, within a period of 
sixty days. 
Sir, if you see the net impact of all these amendments, we have 
appreciated what representatives of Bar Associations and the Law 
Commission had to say, in giving some flexibility in the area of time for filing 
their responses and written statements.  We have added new provisions with 
regard to"the mode of service, so that  those methods could be expedited. We

delegate the function to a Commissioner, if the judge thinks it appropriate to 
do so. 
We have also tried to empower the judge to regulate the time which 
is taken in oral arguments itself. We have also tried to give some indications 
though not a fixed indication that or dinarily, we have given a legislative 
intention or legislative desire that  judgments also should be delivered 
expeditiously, so that the life of each case itself could be compressed, on 
account of these amendments. 
With these few words, Sir, I comm end to this hon. House that this 
amendment Bill be taken into consideration for approval.

look at it from that angle. It is not ju st passing a legislation for the purpose of 
constituting a Haj Committee. Here, I would like to state that the Haj 
Committee can act as a powerful instit ution. It can even mobilise savings and 
investments. It is very important for the hon. Minister to note this. Malaysia is a 
country with a population of about 22 million. And it has a Muslim population of 
about 1.16 million. But it has organised its affairs of Haj management in such 
a way that it is not only helping the pilgrims to go from Malaysia to perform Haj 
in a very orderly manner, but also it has created a habit of saving among those 
who perform Haj. Today, their instit ution, which is similar to our Haj 
Committee, is one of the richest instituti ons with more than Rs.5000 crores of 
funds utilised for the overall benefit of the pilgrims as well as the have-nots in 
the Muslim community. That institution called, Tabung Haji, is similar to our 
Haj Committee under the Haj Act which we are instituting, with a purpose to 
provide mobilising savings, gradually investing in economic activities. Having 
the second largest Muslim population, it is possible for India to mobilise the 
savings through such an institution. The Malaysian example is a unique 
example. They are running airlines, they are running banks, they are making 
profits and subsidising the pilgrims from their own resources which have been 
generated. I have no time to go into t he details of the Malaysian experiment. I 
would only urge the hon. Minister. This Bill has been introduced now. We 
welcome it. But still, there is a need for us to better the Haj management by 
taking cue from the Malaysian experiment. 
Coming to the present Haj Committee, there is a lot to be said about 
the management of the Haj affairs by the present Haj Committee. Sir, it 
handles almost Rs.400 crores  every year of the pilgrims' funds. Parliament is 
not informed on that. The accounts of the Haj Committee are not placed 
before Parliament. It is public money. Thoug h it is constituted under an Act of 
Parliament, none of us knows anything about the balance-

I would request the Government to enlighten me about the rules and 
regulations proposed in the Bill. I would like to know whether action has

like to point out that though the number of pilgrims is increasing, but their 
facilities and benefits are reducing.

being reduced in a phased manner. So, they are not able to meet their needs. 
My third point is regarding the issuance of passport, visa and foreign 
currency. It is centralised at Delhi an d Mumbai. Earlier, the Haj pilgrims 
demanded decentralisation of the system so that they do no t suffer, they are 
not put trouble, and could avail of this fa cility from their home State. If it is 
decentralised, they can easily meet their requirements from their home States 
instead of rushing to Delhi or Mumbai . Therefore, I urge upon the Government 
to consider decentralisation of the prevalent system. 
The Haj pilgrims are facing the following difficulties. First, 
accommodation facilities at Jeddah ar e not comfortable. Second, the 
Government of India deputes 400 officials to Saudi Arabia for two-three 
months during the Haj season, including a 250-member Medical Mission for 
rendering general and medical assistance to Indian pilgrims. But this can 
hardly meet the requirements of the Haj pilgrims. In this connection, Sir, I 
would like to remind you about the fire incident during the last Haj. Some of 
the Indian pilgrims sustained burns and some  died. But, it is a matter of regret

travelling by air or chartered flights is  gradually increasing. The embarkation

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
 SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
and my colleagues, first of all, let me thank our dynamic leader, Chief 
Minister of Tamil Nadu, Puratchi ThaJaivi, who has nominated me as a 
Member of this House. With her blessings, I commence my maiden speech. 
First, I welcome the Bill, and support the Bill also. I want to say something 
about pilgrimage. India is a secular country, which is home to more than 130 
million Muslims.    Indian Muslims constitute the second largest Muslim  
community in the world. The Haj is incumbent upon all adult Muslims of 
sound mind with the necessary physical capacity and financial capability. "" 
Successive Indian Governments have extended assistance to the Indian 
Muslims to perform the Haj. H indicates a commitment of the Government to 
provide all the facilities to enable the I ndian Muslims to fulfil their religious 
obligations smoothly. In this connection, I would like to express my gratitude 
to the Ministry of State for External A ffairs for showing interest in the welfare 
of Haj pilgrims and enhancing t he quota from 65,000 to 72,000 to 
accommodate all applicants from India during Haj-2002. I earnestly hope that 
with the help of Government of India we would enjoy the same facility in the 
coming Haj-2003 season as well. 
The quota for Haj-2002, for Indian pilgrims proceeding for Haj, 
through State Haj Committees, was fixe d at 72,000. This was distributed to 
each State based on its Muslim population. But in some States, the number of 
applications received is much more than the quota allocated to them, while 
some other States have not utilised the q uota fully. Hence, I strongly urge the 
Government of India to allocate the quota based on the average number of 
pilgrims who performed Haj, in the last fi ve years, from each  State, instead of 
fixing quota based on population and reallocating every year based on lesser 
applications received from other States. 
Sir, the State Hajj Committees are deputing about one or two 
representatives to Saudi Arabia for se lection of buildings every year, by 
incurring huge expenditure, as required by  the Government of India. In this 
connection, I wish to point out that a resolution was passed a couple of years 
back, in the All India Haj Conference that the cost of air ticket of one  of the 
members deputed by the State Haj Committees for selection of buildings will 
be reimbursed by the Central Haj Committee, but this resolution has been put 
in a cold storage and has not been implem ented so far. I request that, based 
on the above resolution, the cost of air ticket for one member, at least, may be 
borne by the Central Haj Committee and implemented from Haj-2003 season. 
241 

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
It is learnt that some of the buildings are loca ted on hillocks in which 
Haj pilgrims are accommodated at Mecca. I request that such buildings should 
not be selected in future. 
It is also understood that pilgrims from different States are 
accommodated in single rooms in various buildings. This causes problem in 
the movement of Hajis to Madina and other places in groups, because it takes 
a long time for picking up Hajis from different buildings and causes delay in the 
arrival of Hajis at Madina, thereby depriving them to perform 40 times prayers. 
Hence, it is suggested that pilg rims from each State may be given 
accommodation in buildings located in a cluster, so as to overcome this 
problem. It is also learnt that the Building Selection Team members deputed by 
various State Haj Committees were not allowed to inspect the buildings at 
Madina. As a result, there were a lot of complaints about the quality of 
accommodation at Madina. Hence, it is suggested that the members of 
Building Selection Team be allowed to inspect the buildings at Madina as well, 
and select buildings based on their suitability. 
Sir, the State Haj Committees at  various embarkation points have 
to incur huge expenditure, for making arrangements like transport facility to 
airport ahd back, deployment of seasonal  staff, hiring of v ehicles, telephone, 
fax charges, etc. But the Central Haj Committee reimburses only Rs. 100 
per pilgrim towards transport charges without taking into account other 
actual expenses. State Haj Committees  have been making representations 
in the matter, and it is suggested that  the rate of reimbursement may be 
enhanced from Rs. 100/- to Rs. 150/- per pilgrim so that the deficit could be 
covered. I would also like to point out that some State Haj Committees 
meet their administrative expendit ure from the administrative grant 
sanctioned by their respective State Governments, which is sometimes not 
sufficient to meet the expenses in full. They have to undertake various 
activities, as per the periodic guidelines issued by the Central Haj 
Committee, which include conducting  of qura, wherever necessary, 
conducting   of  inoculation   programme  at  the  district   level,   conducting  
orientation camps, making supporting arrangements for operation of Haj flights 
etc. All these activities require deployment of seasonal staff and involve a huge 
expenditure. This has increased in recent years. It is, therefore, requested that 
the subsidy payable to State Haj Committees towards administrative 
expenditure may be enhanced from Rs.100 to Rs.200 per pilgrim, from the 
coming Haj-2003.

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
Sir, during Haj-2002, the Ministry of External Affairs had called for 
nominations for deputing staff to work in the Indian Haj Offices at Mecca and 
Madina, but very few got selected from  among those nominated by State Haj 
Committees. It is unfortunate that thou gh nominations are called for from 
State Government employees, none of them is selected by the Government of 
India. It is, therefore, su ggested that suitable persons for the posts of Haj 
Officers, Assistant Haj Officers and Haj Assistants may be selected from those 
nominated by State Governments or Stat e Haj Committees, at least from Haj-
2003, so that there will be repres etnation of varous State Government 
employees and pilgrims. As a result, the welfare of the pilgrims could be taken 
care of in a better manner during their stay at Mecca and Madina. 
The Government of India deputes a Medical Mission to Saudi Arabia 
during the Haj season. Though nominati ons are called for from the State 
Governments, very few are selected from among the employees of the State 
Governments. Medical and para-medical staff from other Ministries of the 
Government of India manage to get the deputation. Pilgrims often complain of 
poor service by the medical teams. I, therefore, request that members of the 
Medical Mission may be selected from among those nominated by the State 
Governments and deputed along with the pilgrims from their respective 
States, for a more effective service. 
Regarding deputation of volunteers, the Governmet of India have 
formulated certain guidelines, according to which Government employees 
alone could be deputed as volunteers. The pilgrims need guidance on 
performing religious rituals, as part of Haj. They find that deputation of 
religious scholars as volunteers is also necessary. Hence, I request the 
Government of India to allow religious scholars such as Ulemas to be deputed 
as volunteers, at least up to 50 per cent of the total number. 
It is learnt that pilgrims of each  State are brought under more than 
one Moallim, which causes a great hardship to the pilgrims. It is, therefore, 
suggested that pilgrims from one.State may be allotted to a particular Moallim, 
for ease of coordination and assistance.  The services of the Moallims and 
their response requires a considerable improvement. I request the 
Government of India to take up the ma tter with the Saudi authorities so that 
the services of Moallims can be improved. 
It is seen that some of the officials handling Haj affairs in the Ministry 
of External Affairs and at the Consulate General of India, Jeddah, are not well-
versed in Islamic practices and Haj rituals.   I am sure there is

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
 
no dearth of Muslim officials to be posted there for handling Haj affairs. Hence, 
I request that Muslim officials well-versed in Islamic practices and Haj rituals 
may be posted there for handling Haj affairs. 
 
Beforfe winding up my speech, I want  to mention some of the steps 
taken by our hon. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister. She has announced an amount 
of Rs.52 lakhs for construction of the Wakf Board office in Tamil Nadu. Our 
hon. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister also made arrangements for issue of foreign 
exchange to the pilgrims at their starting point, namely, Chennai itself, instead 
of issuing foreign exchange at Jeddah. I will take just one more minute, Mr. 
Vice-Chairman. Our leader, Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi has nominated two Muslim 
ladies in two essential services, one as the Wakf Board Chairman and the 
other as a Service Commission member. I wholeheartedly support the Bill, I 
also request the Government to extend similar facilities to devotees of other 
religions also. In Tamil Nadu, my Chief Minister has announced a special 
Annadhana scheme. Devotees of the Hindu Religion who go to temples for 
Darshan are given free and sumptuous meals at the temples. This has 
received widespread appreciation from everybody. I request the Central 
Government to help in such programmes of the State with liberal grants. Thank 
you. 
SHRI M.A. KADAR (Tamil Nadu): I thank you, Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, for giving me this opportunity. I wholeheartedly welcome the Bill. I 
sincerely hope that the Bill will achi eve its purpose. It is really heartening 
that the Bill is going to be enacted after a long wait. The Bill has provided 
for six zones. The existing six zones may be increased to ten zones for 
better management. A large number of pilgrims are benefited from Tamil 
Nadu. The selection of Haj pilgrims is  made on the basis of draw of lots. 
Elderly people who are eager to go on Haj pilgrim are sometimes denied 
their chance due to the draw of lots. Therefore, I request that the elderly 
people should be given priority over youngsters. Suitable modifications in the  
selection procedure must be made to enable the elderly people to go on 
pilgrimage. 
In Tamil Nadu, Chennai is the only place of embarking for Haj 
pilgrims. Madurai is the most convenient place for pilgrims from the southern 
part of Tamil Nadu. Madurai has an airpor t. Therefore, I request that Madurai 
should also be made an embarkation point. With these words, I support the 
Bill.  Thank you.

SHRI M. P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Mr. vlce-Chairman, 
Sir, I welcome this Bill, and I congratulat e the hon. Minister for this healthy 
tendency of coming with such an important  Bill which is related to the secular 
credentials, the religious freedom and th e great heritage of our nation. This 
subject is very much related to Islam as a belief, and also to India, as a 
country. Islam considers Haj, as has already been mentioned by hon. 
Members who spoke before me, as one of t he cardinal principles of religion. It 
has two aspects. One aspect is related to the purification of the individual, and 
the other is one of univer sal brotherhood. People cutting across differences of 
caste, nationalities, languages and so on, assemble

there. Sir, Haj is considered as t he biggest international conference where 
people from all nations, languages and so on, assemble, and they declare the 
great motto of universal brotherhood and fraternity. It is nothing but fair and 
nothing but an honour and a privilege for our nation, to send our citizens to 
such a great religious assembly, because our country aJso has many people 
who profess the faith of Islam. And so, I think there is no meaning in linking 
such an issue with the majority and minority problems. It is in no way related to 
the majority and minority problems. It is meaningless to make it controversial, 
especially in this kind of an hour when there is an urgent need throughout the 
country to strengthen our bonds of relationship, our bonds of communal 
harmony and the bonds of fraternity amongst various communities. I think it 
should be considered as an opportunity for introspection. The role of religion, 
whether it is Haj or Teerthyatra, is that of self-realisation; it is that of self-
purification; it is of br otherhood, as Guru Nanak Devji declared. Guru Nanak 
Dev is often considered as a great link between the Hindu brethren and the 
Muslim brethren. He said, if you go for Ha j, you go for Bhakti. Bhakti in Islamic 
terminology, is taqva. I think Guru Nanak used the same terminology, because 
he was very much aware of the terminology  of Islam. At the same time, Guru 
Nanak said, if you go to Ganga, you go with bhakti; when you take a dip in the 
waters of the Ganges, you do it with bhakti; if you don't have bhakti, then there 
is no difference between the frog that is living in the Ganga aad the pious man 
who is going for such a pilgrimage. So, I feel these kinds of things should 
contribute for an inter-community dialogue.  I am not criticising my hon. friend, 
who spoke from the other side, Shri Sh yam Lai. I appreciate that he went into 
the details of it and made a very good speech. He had studied it. But he said 
that the Muslims go for darshan of the Paigambar, Mohammad Saheb; they go 
to see Prophet Mohammad. Actually, it is  not for that. Haj is not for darshan of 
any Prophet or any human being; Haj is for strengthening the belief in God, 
the one God. He has not said it in tentionally. But this is a gross 
misunderstanding that people have. We live in the same country. We drink the 
same water. We breathe the same air. But there are bridges to be built 
between the various communities. So, whether  it is Haj, the Kailash Yatra, the 
Badrinath Yatra or any other thing, these pilgrimages must contribute to a new 
awakening of mutual understanding between the various communities of our 
country. Sir, the issue of Haj, whether it  is the subsidy or the other things, is 
not related to article 25 of the Constitu tion. Every person is entitled to profess, 
to practice and to propagate his religion. It has been provided in the

SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Vice-Cha irman, Sir, I would, at the 
beginning, like to place on record my gratitude to all the Members who have 
participated in this debate. I was fortunate enough to have, in the course of this 
debate, two Members making their maiden speeches. I would like to 
compliment them for the speeches that they made and also for the valid 
suggestions they made during the course of their speeches. This Bilr, that we 
seek to pass in the Rajya Sabha to day, is about the restructuring and 
reconstituting of the Central Haj Co mmittee, the State Haj Committees and 
actions related thereto. It doesn't perta in to the subsidy, flights or the 
arrangements or lack of them in Saudi Arabia. Unfortunately, during the course 
of this debate, somehow, we seem to have gone off tangent and the majority of 
time seems to have been spent either in talking about the arrangements in 
Saudi Arabia and they have gone about or the subsidy, whether it is a good or 
a bad thing. At least, on the subsidy side, Mr. Vice-Chairman, this is an 
argument I do not want to get into. The fa ct is that for the last many years, 
successive Governments have felt that th ere are no options for Hajis in terms 
of travelling to Saudi Arabia. Earlier they  had the option of going over land or 
by sea. Those were the cheaper option s. They exercised those options. So, 
there was no question of subsidy. No w the Saudi Government has closed 
those options and the only option is to travel by air. Successive Governments 
have felt the need to subsidise this ai r travel. And this arrangement has been 
continued by the Government of which I am a member. Having said that, it is 
also the commitment of this Government to explore ways and means and to 
work with both the Central Haj Committ ee and the Muslim leadership of this 
country to see how best this subsidy scheme can be rationalised and to see 
that in due course of time whether it would be possible that all Muslim 
members of this country would be able  to perform Haj without the need for 
subsidy. As a Muslim, I can share with th is House that there is a debate within 
Muslims as to whether this subsidy is  in keeping with our religion or not 
because, as Mirza Abdul Rashid Saheb rightly said, our religion says that Haj 
is only compulsory for those people who are able to perform Haj and able to 
peform not just physically, but able to perform financially also. Therefore, if you 
need subsidy of the Government of I ndia to perform Haj, then are you going 
against the tenets and practices of Islam or not, this is a debate which is going 
on within Islam. But it is out of the contex* of the Centra l Haj Committee Bill. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the Central Haj Committee Bill or rather the Haj 
Committee Act was brought in 1959. At this time all Hajis left by sea and all 
Hajis went from Bombay.  Therefore, the structure of this

Act, the structure of this Central Ha j Committee, the weightage given to 
Maharashtra and particularly to the th en Bombay, now Mumbai, was out of the 
proportion to the rest of the country. Over the years, as I pointed out, the 
transport of Hajis by ship has been replaced with flights. In fact, now this year 
we had 10 embarkation points for Hajis stretching from Srinagar down to 
Hyderabad, Mumbai, Calcutta and numerous ot her cities in Indi a. Therefore, it

longer was Mumbai a pre-eminent place for departure of Hajis, the Central Haj 
Committee Bill or rather the Haj Committee Act would have to be replaced by 
the Central Haj Committee Bill, 2000. This Bill would then seek to correct some 
of the inconsistencies and imbalances that are in place in the existing Act of 
1959. This Bill was placed before the House in 2000. It was presented or 
rather referred to the Standing Committe e on External Affairs. That Committee 
made certain recommendations In fact, they made 23 recommendations for 
alterations to be made to the Bill as it has been presented. I am pleased to 
say, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, that out 23 recommendations, 22 
recommendations have been accepted in toto. One recommendation has been 
accepted partially and that was the re commendation about the shift or rather 
the original Bill of 2000 suggested that  the Central Haj Committee office be 
shifted from Bombay to Delhi in keeping with the move of emphasis away from 
Mumbai and that regional offices be opened. The Government of India, after 
considering this fact, felt because the infrastructure and an enormous Central 
Haj Committee office was already in place in Mumbai, it would be pointless to 
reconstruct a similar office in Delhi and then infrastructure that is already in 
place in Mumbai would go waste. Also, as far as regional offices were 
concerned, it was felt that as of ri ght now, the State Haj Committees were 
doing an excellent job. It was not necessary to have regional offices of the 
Central Haj Committee in various States . But that provision has been kept 
open, and, in case, that need is felt ne cessary, we would get into that as and 
when the need arises. 
Then, the number of pilgrims has increased dramatically, from 24,000 
in 1992 to 72,000 in the year 2002. Along with this, the Central Government, 
working with the Central Haj Committee, has also endeavoured to transfer a lot 
of their responsibilities for the arrangem ents in the run up to the Haj to the 
various State Haj Committees. For example, the draw of lots by which pilgrims 
are selected, or the qura, earlier, was the responsibility of the Central Haj

transferred   to   the   State   Haj   Cdmmittees.      The   pre-

embarkation arrangements, tr ansportation to the embarkation points, provision 
camps, and facilities at such points, all these arrangements have gradually been 
transferred to the State Haj Committees be cause it is felt that the State Haj 
Committees being on the ground right there, will be able to make better 
arrangements. Of course, in a supportive capacity, the Central Haj Committee

accommodation. As a result, sub-standard accommodation is chosen or there is 
some amount of financial impropriety in  the selection of residential units in 
Mecca and Madina. Now, first and foremost, every effort is made to maintain a 
transparent system in the selection of accommodation. The guidelines for 
selection of accommodation are laid down  by the Government of Saudi Arabia, 
in terms of the amount of space to be ma de available. This year, the amount of 
space for the Hajis was increased from 2.5 sq. me ters to 3 sq. meters. Aside 
from that, the guidelines of the Ministry of External Affairs to our officials in 
Saudi Arabia and the accommodation teams that visit there are that no building 
without lift and telephone will be taken on rent for Hajis. To suggest that the 
Central Haj Committee has no role to play in this, is incorrect because what 
happens is, the accommodation is selected jointly by teams of the Central Haj 
Committee as well as officials of the Consulate General of India. For this 
purpose, building selection teams ar e deputed. The State Haj Committee 
officials also go to Mecca. They select buildings as per the pre-set norms for this 
purpose. Rooms are measured. Buildings are taken on the basis of the number 
of pilgrims. As I mentioned, no buildings are taken without lift or telephone 
facility, and they must fall within the prescribed distance from Harin Sharief. 
After the buildings are identified, a me mber of the Haj Committee visits Mecca 
Sharief and goes through each of these selections, visits each of the buildings, 
ensures that - the guidelines  that are laid down are being followed, and makes 
sure that the Hajis get the best possible accommodation. Wherever problem 
arises with the accommodation, is  not with the pre-set numbers of Hajis, for 
which the officials in Saudi Arabia receive prior notice. It is when at the last 
minute, sometimes, the * Central Haj Committee sends people from the waiting 
list, and, within a few days' notice, a sks our officials in Mecca and Madina to 
make accommodation available, then we have to settle for a lower category of 
accommodation because, otherwise, we are accused of

be present in Saudi Arabia continuously. It is not possible for them to have a

MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 621, Question Nos. 623 and 627 are 
also similar. They are al so on the unorganised labour sector. So, we take 
them up together. 
Workshop on Unorganized Labour Sector 
†*621. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a two day workshop on unorganized labour sector was held 
at Bhopal which was addressed by the renowned economists and social 
scientists; 
(b) if so, the recommendations of the workshop; and 
(c) Government's response on these recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (c) 
Yes, Sir. A two-day workshop on "The Unorganized Sector in Madhya 
Pradesh" was organized by a Non-Governmental Organization, called the 
Institute for Human Development on 1-2nd April, 2002 at Bhopal. As per the 
information received from the Government of Madhya Pradesh, they have not 
yet formally received the recommenda tions from the organizers of the 
Workshop. 
Growth of employment in Organized/Unorganized sectors  . 
†*623. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the rate of growth of employment in the organized and 
†Starred question Nos. 621, 623 and 627 were taken together. 
 
1

RAJYA  SABHA [9 May, 2002] 
unorganized sectors, separately, in co mparison to the previous three years, 
State-wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that during 2001-02, 50 lakh jobs have been lost 
in the organized/unorganized sectors; and 
(c) the manner in which Government propose to address the problem 
of educated unemployed? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (c) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The rate of growth of employment in the organized and unorgazined 
sectors for major States and at National level is given in the statement. (See 
below) 
Though the rate of growth in employment in the organized sector has 
declined by 0.5% during 1999-2000, there is an increase in the growth rate in 
the unorganized sector. While job opportunities declined in certain sectors, 
new jobs are being created in many emerging sectors like Information 
Technology, Tourism, Construction etc. On the whole, the economy achieved 
a growth rate of around 0.98% in employment. 
The approach to the Tenth Plan focusses on providing gainful high 
quality employment to the additions to the labour force and it is listed as one 
of the monitorable objectives for the Tenth Plan and beyond. The growth 
strategy of the Tenth Plan would lay emphasis on rapid growth of those 
sectors which are likely to create high quality employment opportunities and 
deal with the policy constraints which discourage growth of employment. 
Particular attention would be paid to the policy environment influencing a 
wide range of economic activities which have a large employment potential.

†*627. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state the action taken to  protect interests of the unorganized 
farm labourers? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
To protect the interests of workers including unorganized agricultural 
workers, the Government has enacted the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the 
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 
1976 and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditions of Service) Act, 1979. A so cial security scheme namely, 'Krishi 
Shramik^Samajik Suraksha Yojana-2000' has also been launched in selected 
50 districts in the country with the obj ective of covering 10 lakh agricultural 
workers over a period of three years. The scheme envisages to provide through 
Life Insurance Corporati on of India, life-cum-acci dent insurance, money-
back, pension and superannuation benefits. Jan Shri Bima Yojana is also in 
operation for those below the poverty line or marginally above the poverty 
line which inter-alia includes agricultural labourers. Some other schemes for 
the welfare of rural workers includ ing agricultural workers are Pradhan 
Mantri Gramodaya Yojana Swarnjayan ti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY), 
Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY), Employment Assurance Scheme 
(EAS), National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) etc.
